id: I Ask My Grandmother What Trinidad Was Like in 1960

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Paradise with a thousand stings, she replies. Deep blue and blazing sky. Incessant cicadas, scuttle of bug and roach. Fleas, mosquitos, the threat of scorpions. Men leaning on doorposts, crowding the bar. Smoking, drinking, laughing descendants of slaves. Fire coral burns, reef-edge barracudas. Truly lovely. Matriarchal, she says, women with eight children by many different men. The men would leave as the spirit took them. I want to know all the forces one can call spirit. Tall, swaying fronds of the sugar cane fields. Distant roar heralding a downpour. Snapping turtles. Nearby shanty town, she says, streets full of rubbish, rats in the gutter. I admired the colonial-style homes, she says. Colonial, I say. Separate servant quarters and grounds filled with samaan trees, the balconies overflowing with hot-colored orchids and the locusts drawn close by the palatial lights, colorful and clawing, their hooks sunk deep into the bare skin of a sweating back.

An Eden riddled with stinging things, she tells me. Sky burning blue overhead. Cicadas that never quiet, roaches and insects darting past. Scorpions lurking as a constant worry, mosquitos and fleas everywhere. Bar-goers and men propped against doorframes. Laughter, cigarettes, drinks shared among those descended from bondage. Barracudas patrol the reef's edge while fire coral scalds. Genuinely beautiful, though. Society here runs through the mothers, she explains—women raising eight kids fathered by a rotating cast of men. Whenever the impulse struck them, the fathers simply departed. I find myself wondering what forces deserve the name "spirit." Sugarcane stalks bending and rustling in tall rows. Thunder rolling in from a distance, promising rain. Turtles that snap. A slum sits close by, she mentions, its roads littered with trash, rodents moving through the drains. She confesses her fondness for the old colonial houses. Colonial, I repeat back. Quarters once meant for servants stand apart from the main grounds, samaan trees shading the property, balconies spilling over with vivid orchids, and locusts pulled toward the grand lighting—vibrant, grasping insects whose barbs dig into damp, exposed shoulders.
outputs.L3:
# Paradise and Its Perils: A Study of Beauty and Exploitation in an Island Narrative

The narrator's evocative characterization of the island as "paradise with a thousand stings" establishes the central tension that permeates the entire narrative. This phrase captures the fundamental duality of the setting—a place of extraordinary natural splendor that simultaneously harbors constant threats to those who inhabit it. The lush, vibrant landscape that might appear idyllic to outside observers conceals numerous dangers: fire coral lurking beneath seemingly pristine waters ready to sear unsuspecting skin, scorpions hiding in the shadows of tropical vegetation, and swarms of biting insects that torment both body and spirit. This juxtaposition serves as more than mere descriptive flourish; it functions as a metaphorical framework through which the narrator examines the island's social fabric, suggesting that beneath the surface beauty of this tropical world lie wounds both literal and figurative.

This duality extends powerfully into the realm of social organization, where the narrator depicts a distinctly matriarchal society. Women in this community bear the primary responsibility of raising numerous children fathered by different men—men who depart without warning or explanation, moving on "as the spirit took them." This casual, almost mystical framing of male abandonment prompts the narrator to interrogate the nature of this so-called spirit. What forces, the narrator wonders, truly compel these men to leave? Is it genuine wanderlust, economic necessity, social conditioning, or something more insidious—a pattern of behavior normalized by generations of transient relationships? The narrator's questioning tone suggests skepticism toward this seemingly natural explanation, hinting that larger structural forces—perhaps rooted in the island's colonial history and economic disparities—may be disguised as mere personal whim or restless spirit.

The narrative's social commentary sharpens considerably when the narrator turns attention to the island's stark class divisions. On one side exists the impoverished shanty town, its streets choked with rubbish and populated by scavenging rats, a visceral testament to poverty's grip on much of the population. This squalor stands in jarring contrast to the colonial-style homes that dot the landscape—grand residences admired for their architectural elegance and, tellingly, their separate servant quarters. This physical separation between master and servant spaces within the same properties speaks volumes about the entrenched hierarchies that structure island life, hierarchies inherited from colonial systems that persist long after formal colonial rule has ended or transformed.

The narrator's descriptions of these colonial estates reveal grounds of remarkable beauty: towering samaan trees providing generous shade, orchids blooming in vivid, arresting colors that seem to embody the island's tropical abundance. Yet even here, in these manicured and privileged spaces, the "thousand stings" motif reasserts itself. Locusts, drawn inexorably to the palatial lights that illuminate these grand homes after dark, become instruments of minor torment—their claws digging into sweating backs, perhaps those of servants or laborers who maintain these beautiful grounds while remaining excluded from the comforts within. This image powerfully encapsulates how privilege and suffering coexist in the same physical space, how the very light that signals wealth and comfort also attracts irritation and pain for those whose bodies bear the marks of their labor.

Throughout the text, the narrator weaves natural imagery seamlessly with these social observations, creating a rich tapestry that reveals deeper truths about exploitation and beauty existing in constant tension. The rhythmic chorus of cicadas provides an ambient soundtrack to daily life, while fields of sugar cane—historically the very crop that drove colonial exploitation and the transatlantic slave trade—stretch across the landscape as both agricultural necessity and haunting reminder of historical trauma. Sudden tropical downpours punctuate the narrative, offering both refreshment and disruption, while turtles making their ancient journeys to nesting grounds symbolize continuity and natural cycles that persist regardless of human social arrangements.

Through this careful interweaving of natural and social imagery, the narrator constructs a complex portrait of island life that refuses simple categorization. The paradise is real, but so are its stings—both literal, in the form of dangerous creatures and insects, and metaphorical, in the form of social inequities, absent fathers, and the enduring shadows of colonial exploitation. This narrative technique ultimately suggests that true understanding of this island world requires acknowledging both its extraordinary beauty and its persistent wounds, recognizing that these elements are not contradictory but rather fundamentally intertwined aspects of the same complex reality.
outputs.L4:
# The Weight of Paradise

The mosquitoes arrived first, before the sun had fully committed to rising, needling through the thin mesh of the veranda screens with a persistence that mirrored the island itself—beautiful, relentless, drawing blood without apparent malice. Rosalie slapped at her forearm and cursed softly in patois, the words dissolving into the humid air like sugar in rum.

"Mama, look," called her daughter Esperanza from the garden below, holding up an orchid the color of a bruise healing—purple shot through with yellow, delicate as tissue paper yet somehow obscene in its beauty. "It grew right through the fence."

Rosalie leaned over the railing, taking in the flower and, beyond it, the tin roofs of the shanty town that sprawled down toward the harbor like an afterthought the island had never quite forgiven itself for. Smoke rose from cooking fires there, thin gray ribbons twisting up into a sky so relentlessly blue it seemed to mock the poverty beneath it. Somewhere a rooster crowed, absurdly late, and somewhere else a radio crackled with reggae static.

"That flower grew through the fence because nothing on this island respects a boundary," Rosalie said. "Not the plants, not the men, not the weather."

Esperanza laughed, but there was an edge to it. At sixteen, she had already learned the particular arithmetic of the island: how beauty and hardship shared the same soil, drew from the same rain, breathed the same salt-heavy air. She had learned it from her mother, who had learned it from her mother before her—three generations of women running households in the absence of men who had gone to sea, gone to America, gone simply gone, swallowed by opportunities that never seemed to circle back this way.

"Papa called last night," Esperanza said, testing the words like stepping onto reef rock, uncertain if it would hold.

Rosalie's hands stilled on the porch rail. Below, a lizard skittered across sun-warmed stone, its throat pulsing orange—a small violent heartbeat visible to anyone who cared to look. "Did he now."

"He says he's sending money. For the roof."

"He always says that." Rosalie's voice carried no bitterness, only the flat weariness of repetition, the particular fatigue of a woman who had heard promises evaporate like morning dew a hundred times before. "The roof leaked through three rainy seasons already. We fixed it ourselves, your grandmother and I, with our own hands and Mr. Charles's tin sheets he had left over from his chicken coop."

This was the island's secret architecture: women building shelter from scraps while men's promises floated somewhere over the horizon, indistinguishable from the heat shimmer that made the sea seem to boil at midday.

They could see, from their hillside perch, the old plantation house that crowned the opposite ridge—white columns rising from emerald lawns like teeth, indifferent and gleaming, a monument to a history everyone acknowledged and no one quite discussed at dinner. The Beaumont family had owned it since before emancipation, and owned it still, though now they called it a "heritage property" and rented rooms to tourists who wanted authentic Caribbean charm without authentic Caribbean complications. The irony sat in the valley between the two homes like fog that never quite burned off.

"Grandmother says the Beaumonts' great-great-grandfather owned this land," Esperanza said. "All of it. Even where our house sits."

"He owned the people who worked it too," Rosalie replied. "Some things don't wash away just because time passes. The stain sinks into the ground. You plant something new, and it still comes up marked."

Down in the shanty town, a woman's laughter rose above the general murmur—rich, unbothered, defiantly joyful despite everything the morning implied about the day's labor ahead. This was the island's other secret: that joy did not wait for justice, that celebration bloomed in cracked concrete same as the orchids bloomed through fences. Music drifted up from somewhere, a steel drum finding its rhythm, careless of history, insistent on the present moment.

Rosalie's mother emerged onto the veranda then, moving slowly, her joints complaining in the way they always did before the true heat arrived. She carried a plate of fried plantains, their edges caramelized dark and sweet, and set them down without ceremony.

"You two are talking about men again," she said. It wasn't a question.

"Papa called," Esperanza offered.

The old woman made a sound in her throat—not quite dismissal, not quite acceptance, something worn smooth by decades of similar calls, similar promises, similar silences that followed. "Eat something," she said instead. "The plantains won't wait for foolishness."

They ate in comfortable silence, the three of them, while below the island continued its complicated performance: beauty and poverty, colonial ghosts and vibrant life, absent fathers and present grandmothers, all woven together so thoroughly that separating one thread from another seemed not just difficult but somehow false, a betrayal of the truth that paradise, wherever it existed, always came at a cost someone had already paid, was still paying, would likely go on paying long after the tourists had photographed their orchids and gone home satisfied with their glimpse of the beautiful, uncomplicated tropics.

The mosquitoes returned as the morning wore on, indifferent to metaphor, interested only in blood. Rosalie slapped at her arm again, this time without cursing, simply accepting it as one more small tax levied by a land that gave so generously and demanded, always, its due in return.
outputs.L5:
# Paradise, Deep, Incessant

There is a paradise that exists not above the clouds, but somewhere deep within—a place accessed only when the incessant noise of daily life finally quiets. We spend so much of our existence chasing distractions, filling every silence with sound, every stillness with motion, that we forget paradise was never meant to be found. It was meant to be uncovered.

The deep is where truth lives. Not the shallow deep of ocean trenches or buried treasure, but the deep of the self—the parts of us that remain untouched by trends, unmoved by the incessant demands of notifications and obligations and the constant hum of other people's expectations. To go deep requires descending past the surface chatter, past the performance we give the world, into something quieter and more honest.

But descent is not comfortable. The incessant pull of habit drags us back toward the surface again and again. We check the phone. We fill the silence. We convince ourselves that busyness is purpose, that noise is aliveness. And so paradise remains just out of reach—not because it's hidden in some distant land, but because we refuse to sit still long enough to find it within ourselves.

Perhaps paradise isn't a destination at all. Perhaps it's simply what remains when the incessant noise finally stops—when we stop performing, stop scrolling, stop running from the deep parts of ourselves that ask for attention. In that stillness, briefly, we might glimpse it: not a place with golden gates, but a feeling. Enoughness. Presence. The quiet understanding that we were never far from paradise—we were only ever too loud to notice it was already here.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem in a dialogue-fragment style about a Caribbean island, blending beauty and decay, colonialism and nature imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Sea Keeps

"Tell me again," she says, "about the water."

The water was turquoise once, before the word *turquoise* became a paint chip in a hotel lobby, before they named a drink after the color and forgot the color came from something alive.

"And the sugar."

The sugar came from cane, and the cane came from blood, though the brochures say *paradise* and *pristine* and *untouched*, as if six generations of touching hadn't happened, as if the touching wasn't still happening in the kitchens where the workers make eleven dollars an hour to serve rum to men whose grandfathers owned the island's grandfathers.

*Look at the light,* they say. *Have you ever seen light like this?*

The light is the same light it always was. The light doesn't know about ownership. The light falls equally on the crumbling great house—vines threading through its ribs like it's being slowly eaten by something patient and green—and on the resort next door, all glass and infinity pools that pretend the ocean isn't already infinite, doesn't need our help pretending.

"What happened to the church?"

Termites. Salt air. A hundred and forty years of hurricanes. The roof caved in sometime in the eighties and nobody rebuilt it because the congregation had already scattered—to Miami, to Brooklyn, to wherever the checks came from that kept the family land from being sold to men in linen suits who talk about *authentic experiences.*

*Authentic,* she repeats, tasting the word like it might be poison.

The flamboyant trees don't care. They bloom red-orange-violent every June whether or not anyone's there to call it beautiful. The beauty was never for us. It was just weather, biology, the tree doing what trees do, and we arrived after, calling it Eden, calling it ours, calling it a bargain at four hundred dollars a night.

"Do you think it remembers?"

The soil remembers. Dig anywhere and you'll hit bone, shell, ballast stone from ships that came empty and left full, or came full and left empty—depends which crossing you mean. The soil doesn't forget. It just grows things anyway. Bougainvillea doesn't apologize. The mango tree in the old slave quarters' yard still drops fruit every August, sweet and orange and completely indifferent to what the ground beneath it holds.

*Isn't it beautiful, though?*

Yes. That's the terrible part. Yes, unbearably. The way the ruins get better with age, more photogenic, moss finding the cracks in the colonial stone like it's dressing a wound. Yes, the water is that blue. Yes, the light does that thing at five p.m. Yes, you can stand in the old fort and watch the sun go down and feel something crack open in your chest that might be grief and might be wonder and is probably, unbearably, both.

"So what do we do with that?"

We drink the rum. We eat the mango. We let the light do what light does.

We remember anyway.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a piece of literary fiction using two unnamed voices exchanging impressions of a tropical island, mixing sensory detail with social commentary on race and class.
counterfactuals.output:
# Two Voices, One Shore

**I.**

The water here is the color they put on postcards, she said, the kind of blue that makes you suspicious of your own eyes. I stood on the balcony this morning with my coffee and watched a man rake the sand into perfect lines, over and over, erasing footprints before the guests woke to make them again.

**II.**

I saw him too. Same man, maybe, or one just like him—there's a uniform for that kind of invisibility, pale blue shirt, the island's name embroidered where a heart would be. My father raked sugar cane on an island like this one, different flag, same blue shirt practically. He used to say the tourists paid for two things: the view, and not having to see who maintained it.

**I.**

We ate lunch at a place recommended by the concierge. Fish so fresh it seemed almost rude to eat it, like interrupting something. The woman who served us had a gold tooth that caught the light every time she smiled, and she smiled constantly, professionally, the way you'd tune an instrument. I left a large tip and felt the particular guilt of the adequately paid.

**II.**

Adequate guilt. That's good. I've felt that. There's a whole economy of feeling here, isn't there—the guilt calibrated to exactly the size of the check, dissolving by the second gin and tonic. I watched a family, white, sunburned already by ten a.m., order the "local specialty," and the staff performed authenticity for them like actors who'd rehearsed being themselves.

**I.**

The hotel brochure called it "unspoiled." I keep turning that word over. Unspoiled by what, exactly. Not by the four hundred rooms stacked like teeth along the shore. Not by us. Something else, something that happened before, that they've managed to launder out of the language. The pool boy—I hate that phrase, pool boy, he's a grown man with a wedding ring—told me his grandmother remembers when this beach had a different name, one that isn't on any map now.

**II.**

They renamed the whole coast for the resorts. There's a version of the water that existed before it became "the color they put on postcards." I think about that a lot—how the beauty was always here, and now it's been repackaged, sold back to the descendants of the people who first called it beautiful, except now they're the ones raking the sand.

**I.**

Yesterday a boat went by, not a tourist boat, just a fishing boat, low in the water, patched sail. Everyone on our beach turned to look, and I heard someone say, isn't that charming, and I understood suddenly that charming was doing a lot of work in that sentence. Charming meant: poor, but photogenic. Charming meant: I will not have to know these people, only admire them from a distance, the way you admire weather.

**II.**

I keep thinking about the word paradise. Who gets to live inside it and who gets to clean it. There's a hierarchy built into the architecture itself—guest rooms facing the water, staff quarters facing the road, and everyone too polite, or too paid, to mention the difference.

**I.**

At dinner last night the band played something they called "authentic island music," four men in matching shirts, and afterward a British couple asked to take a photo with them, and the men smiled that same tuned smile, and I thought: this is a transaction too, though no one's counting it as one.

**II.**

We'll go home with our tans and our photographs and call it a vacation. They'll go home—if home is even the word, if home isn't just the other side of a fence we didn't notice—to the part of the island that isn't in the brochure. I don't know what to do with that except notice it, which feels like nothing, which is probably why I keep saying it out loud, to you, on this balcony, over coffee that someone else grew and someone else picked and someone else brought to me on a tray, smiling.

**I.**

The water is still that impossible blue. I don't think it's lying. I think it's just older than all of this, older than the flags and the resorts and the renaming, and it doesn't know yet that it's supposed to mean something different depending on which side of the beach you're standing on.

**II.**

Maybe that's the only honest thing here. The water doesn't perform for anyone. It just keeps being blue, indifferent to who's watching, indifferent to who's raking the sand beneath it into lines that will not last the hour.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical, fragmented narrative about someone recalling a Caribbean island's paradise-like qualities alongside its darker colonial history, using recurring insect and plant imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Sea Keeps

I.

The bougainvillea climbs the colonial wall
the way memory climbs a throat—
uninvited, flowering anyway.

My grandmother said: *this earth remembers
what we try to forget.*

She meant the cane fields.
She meant the mosquitoes that carried fever
into the blood of men who came
with muskets and Bibles and hunger
shaped like ownership.

II.

Hummingbirds thread the hibiscus like needles
mending something that cannot be mended—

*mending anyway.*

There is a sound the cicadas make at dusk,
a rising chorus, relentless,
that could be joy
or could be warning,
and no one has ever told me
how to tell the difference.

III.

The great house still stands, whitewashed,
its verandas open to trade winds
that once carried ships heavy with people
made into cargo, made into ledger lines,
made into *fifty souls, deliverable, healthy stock.*

The frangipani blooms there still.
Sweet almost to the point of grief.
Petals falling like something
too soft to be punishment
and yet.

IV.

I remember the sand, white as bone,
the water so clear you could see
your own feet standing in it,
rooted like mangroves,
like the ones who couldn't leave,
like the ones who were never allowed to.

Someone told me once
that mangroves hold the shoreline together—
their roots a fist beneath the water,
gripping what would otherwise
wash away.

V.

Ants build their empire in the cracks
of the old sugar mill, its stone teeth
broken now, its machinery
rusted into abstraction—

but the ants don't know history.
They only know the sweetness left behind,
the way sugar seeps into everything,
into soil, into blood,
into the very language
we use to name this place:
*paradise, paradise, paradise*—

as if a word could be a kind of forgetting.

VI.

At night, the fireflies rise from the grass
like small ideas trying to become bright enough
to matter.

I think of the enslaved who ran,
who used firelight and darkness both
as maps,
as prayers,
as the only cartography available
to the body seeking its own freedom.

The insects don't remember this.
Only the land does,
in its silence,
in the way roots still search
for water beneath the surface,
the way everything living
keeps looking
for what was taken.

VII.

Here is the paradox I was given
instead of a homeland:

turquoise water, poison history.
Golden light, ledgers of loss.
The scent of nutmeg and clove
mixed with something
that will not wash out,
however far the tide comes in.

VIII.

My grandmother, again:
*this is why the flowers grow so loud here—
they are singing over something.*

The trumpet vine.
The orchid, orange as a wound.
The bright, insistent bougainvillea
that will not stop climbing
even now,
even here,
even knowing
what the walls were built to hold.

IX.

I return each year
to the beach where my ancestors
were not permitted to walk as free people,
where now children run screaming
with joy into the surf,
unburdened, or so it seems,
though the mosquitoes still bite
in the old patterns,
the palms still bend
in the old hurricanes,
the sea still holds
its terrible, turquoise memory.

X.

What I know: the beauty is not a lie.
What I know: the horror is not erased.

They exist together
the way the cicada's song exists
both as music
and as warning,

the way sugar can sweeten
and also rot,

the way an island can be
a grave
and a garden
in the very same breath—

each bloom
a small rebellion
against the forgetting
the world
keeps asking it
to do.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a short experimental prose piece structured as overheard conversation, describing an island's wildlife, weather, and inhabitants, with an undercurrent of critique about colonial architecture and inequality.
counterfactuals.output:
# Fragments from the Veranda

"—no, the parrots come at dusk, not dawn, whoever told you that hasn't been listening—"

*(the rain arrives sideways here, testing the seams of every roof, and some roofs, you understand, were built to fail)*

"—my grandmother says the iguanas remember which houses used to be theirs. The old sugar estate, the one with columns like it's Athens transplanted, that's where they sun themselves on the steps most mornings. Fitting, no?"

"—you're being dramatic—"

"—I'm being *accurate*. There's a difference. Pass the coffee—"

*(three species of hummingbird, and only one has a name in the language spoken here before the ships came; the others were named after men who never learned to pronounce the mountains)*

"—the hurricane season starts earlier each year, the fishermen say, though who keeps records anymore, who writes it down except in the body, in the ache before the barometric drop—"

"—my uncle worked forty years laying stone for the hotel wing, the one with the view, the one none of us can afford to sleep in—"

"—hush, they'll hear you—"

"—let them. The egrets don't care whose money paved the causeway. They stand in the same brackish water regardless, one leg, patient, white as a communion dress, white as the plantation house that's a museum now, that charges admission to see how *they* used to live, no mention of how *we* still do—"

*(the wind has a name too, several, depending on which elder you ask, and none of them match what the meteorologists call it on the mainland broadcast, garbled through static, always arriving late, always announcing the storm after it's already rattled every door)*

"—the parrots, though. Tell me about the parrots again—"

"—they roost in the mahogany that's left, what they didn't cut down for ship masts three centuries back, and every evening they scream like they're arguing about something urgent, something we should probably be listening to—"

"—what do you think they're saying?"

"—I think they're saying *whose island, whose island, whose island*—"

*(and the tide comes in anyway, indifferent, licking at both the servants' quarters and the great house steps with the same patient tongue, the same rising, the same eventual claim)*
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a vivid, sensory description of an island paradise that subtly reveals its colonial past and social contradictions, using poetic, run-on sentences and shifting perspectives.
counterfactuals.output:
The island announces itself before you see it—salt and frangipani and something charred underneath, like sugar burning in a pan someone forgot, and the water goes through every blue that has a name and several that don't, turquoise sliding into cobalt sliding into a green so bright it seems manufactured, and the brochures call this *unspoiled*, though nothing here has ever been left alone, not the reefs combed smooth by generations of hands, not the palms planted in rows too straight to be accidental, marching down to the shore like something that was once given an order and never stopped obeying it.

Look how the light falls through the canopy in cathedral shafts, dust motes turning to gold, and somewhere a bell is ringing though there is no church you can see from here, only the sound carrying the way sound does in humid air, thick and slow, and you might mistake it for peace if you didn't know that bells like this once meant *muster*, once meant *the ship has come*, once meant six hundred people standing in a line that ended in a hold that smelled of nothing you'd want to remember, and the sea that carried them is the same sea licking at your ankles now, warm as bathwater, forgiving as amnesia—

—and the old woman selling shells on the beach road has her grandmother's hands, cracked like the coral she gathers, and she calls you *sir* in the English that was beaten into her mother's mouth two generations back, English that sits now like a borrowed dress, ill-fitting but worn because the alternative was worse, was silence, was the whip, and she smiles because smiling is also a kind of currency here, has been since the first ships anchored and called this place *discovered*, as though it hadn't been breathing and singing and burying its dead for ten thousand years before that—

The resort rises white as a wedding cake on the bluff where the old plantation house used to stand, and if you dig in the garden—don't, they'll stop you, there's a fine—you'll find brick and bone and the ash-black remains of cane fields burned each harvest for three hundred years, smoke that settled into the soil the way grief settles into a family, quietly, permanently, becoming part of what grows there, and what grows there now is bougainvillea, impossibly purple, impossibly alive, planted by the same hands that used to cut the cane, paid now in different coin though the coin is never quite enough—

Evening comes down like a curtain the color of a bruise healing, mango and violet and a deepening blue, and the tourists gather for cocktails named after pirates and gods, and the band plays songs their great-grandfathers played for masters who called it *entertainment*, called it *quaint*, and somewhere past the pool lights, past the manicured hedge that hides the staff quarters from the ocean view, a woman is singing to her child in a language older than the island's new name, a lullaby that has survived shipwreck and whip and forgetting, and the waves keep arriving the way they always have, indifferent, patient, folding themselves onto the sand over and over like something trying, endlessly, to erase a footprint that was never really gone—

and this too is paradise, this weight beneath the postcard, this history breathing under the sunscreen and the coconut oil, this island that has learned, the way survivors learn, to be beautiful and wounded in the very same breath.
